title: Pallantis virtus. Halaesus et Lausus
titleEn: Pallas Rallies the Arcadians — Aeneid X.362–438
source: P. Vergilius Maro, Aeneid, ed. J. B. Greenough, The Bucolics, Aeneid, and Georgics of Virgil (Boston: Ginn & Company, 1881), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0690.phi003.perseus-lat2, sha256 e639e6a0e27427ef. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Greenough's spelling kept (volnus, divom, Karthago, -is accusatives); his quotation marks printed as “ ”. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: On another part of the field, where a mountain torrent has left the ground strewn with boulders and uprooted trees, the Arcadian cavalry have had to leave their horses, and, unused to fighting on foot, they turn and run from the Latins. Pallas, Evander's young son, shames and pleads with them: the enemy are mortal men like themselves, the sea is at their backs, and the only road home runs through the thickest of the enemy. Then he leads the way and kills man after man: Lagus as he wrenches up a rock, Hisbo who rushes him in fury, Anchemolus who had defiled his stepmother's bed, and the twin sons of Daucus, whom even their parents could not tell apart until Pallas made them different. His men take heart and close up behind him, as scattered fires a shepherd sets merge into one line of flame. On the Italian side Halaesus, whose prophet father had once hidden him in the woods to cheat his fate, cuts down Pallas's men, until Pallas prays to Father Tiber and kills him with a spear. Lausus, son of Mezentius, steadies the Italians, and the two armies lock together, Pallas on one side, Lausus on the other, two young men of rare beauty, neither of whom will ever see home again. Jupiter does not let them meet: each is to die at the hands of a greater enemy.

sentences.t:
At parte ex alia, qua saxa rotantia late
impulerat torrens arbustaque diruta ripis,
sentences.l:
But on another side, where boulders rolling far and wide
had driven a torrent, and trees torn from the banks,
sentences.i: But on another part of the field, where a torrent had sent boulders rolling far and wide, and trees torn from its banks,
sentences.n: A new paragraph in Greenough. 'At', 'but', turns the story from Aeneas's landing to another part of the battle. 'parte ex alia', 'from another side', the preposition placed between adjective and noun, as often in verse. 'qua', 'where'. 'saxa rotantia', 'rolling rocks'; 'impulerat torrens', 'a torrent had driven (them)', pluperfect: the flood has gone and left its wreckage. 'arbusta diruta ripis', 'trees torn from the banks', 'ripis' an ablative of separation. The Latin Library has 'intulerat', 'had carried in', to almost the same sense. Elision 'part(e) ex'.

sentences.t:
Arcadas insuetos acies inferre pedestris
ut vidit Pallas Latio dare terga sequaci
(aspera quis natura loci dimittere quando
suasit equos), unum quod rebus restat egenis,
nunc prece, nunc dictis virtutem accendit amaris:
sentences.l:
the Arcadians, unused to bringing on battle-lines on foot,
when Pallas saw them give their backs to pursuing Latium
(since the rugged nature of the place had persuaded them to let go
their horses), the one thing that is left in needy straits,
now with prayer, now with words bitter he kindles their courage:
sentences.i: when Pallas saw his Arcadians, who were not used to fighting on foot, turning their backs to the pursuing Latins (the rough ground had made them leave their horses), he did the one thing left in such straits, and fired their courage, now with entreaty, now with bitter words:
sentences.n: Pallas, Evander's young son, was put in Aeneas's charge in Book VIII with Evander's Arcadian horsemen. 'Arcadas', Greek accusative plural. 'insuetos… inferre', 'unused to bringing on', with the infinitive; 'acies… pedestris', 'battle on foot', accusative plural in '-is'. 'ut vidit', 'when he saw', 'ut' with the perfect indicative. 'Latio… sequaci', 'to pursuing Latium', the land for its people; 'dare terga', 'to give their backs', to run. In the parenthesis 'quis' is the old dative plural of the relative (= 'quibus'), 'to whom', and 'quando' means 'since'. The Latin Library has 'aquis': 'the nature of the place, rough with water', with no relative. 'unum quod… restat', 'the one thing that remains', in apposition to what follows. Elision 'virtut(em) accendit'.

sentences.t: “Quo fugitis, socii?
sentences.l: “Where are you fleeing, comrades?
sentences.i: “Where are you running, my comrades?
sentences.n: Pallas's speech begins with a rebuke. 'Quo', 'to where?', 'whither?'. 'socii', vocative. The whole speech is modelled on Ajax's appeal to the Greeks at the ships in the Iliad: is there a walled city behind us to fall back on? we are far from home with the sea at our backs; our safety lies in our hands (Iliad 15.733–741). No elisions.

sentences.t:
Per vos et fortia facta,
per ducis Evandri nomen devictaque bella
Opemque meam, patriae quae nunc subit aemula laudi,
fidite ne pedibus.
sentences.l:
By yourselves and your brave deeds,
by your leader Evander's name and the wars he fought out,
and my hope, which now rises to rival my father's glory,
do not trust your feet.
sentences.i: By yourselves and your brave deeds, by the name of your leader Evander and the wars he fought and won, by my own hope, which now rises to match my father's fame, do not trust to your feet.
sentences.n: The print has 'Opemque', a misprint for 'spemque', corrected here. 'Opem' cannot open a hexameter, since its first syllable is short ('ŏpis'), and Greenough capitalises only at a stop or for a name; 'spemque', which the Latin Library prints, scans. 'Per… per', 'by…', the form of earnest entreaty. 'devicta bella', 'wars fought to a finish', from 'devinco'. 'patriae… aemula laudi', 'rivalling my father's glory', 'patriae' the adjective 'paternal', 'laudi' dative with 'aemula'; 'subit', 'rises, comes up'. 'fidite ne pedibus' = 'ne fidite', a prohibition with 'ne' and the imperative, a poetic and old-fashioned turn (prose says 'nolite fidere'); 'pedibus' is dative (or ablative) with 'fido'. Trusting their feet means running away, a gibe at horsemen now on foot. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Ferro rumpenda per hostis
est via.
sentences.l:
With steel must be burst through the enemy
the way.
sentences.i: Our road runs through the enemy, and it must be cut open with the sword.
sentences.n: 'rumpenda est via', a gerundive of obligation: 'a way is to be burst open', 'a way must be broken'. 'ferro', ablative of means, 'with the sword'. 'per hostis', accusative plural in '-is'. The line break throws 'est via' to the head of the next line, short and emphatic. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Qua globus ille virum densissimus urget,
hac vos et Pallanta ducem patria alta reposcit.
sentences.l:
Where that mass of men, thickest, presses,
there you and Pallas your leader your lofty homeland demands back.
sentences.i: Where that knot of men presses thickest, that is the road by which our homeland, high on its hill, demands you back, you and Pallas your leader.
sentences.n: 'Qua… hac', 'by which way… by this way'. 'globus', 'a ball', a dense knot of soldiers; 'densissimus', 'thickest'. 'virum' = 'virorum', the old genitive plural you have met often. 'Pallanta', Greek accusative of 'Pallas': he names himself, as their commander. 'patria alta', 'your lofty homeland', Evander's town Pallanteum on the Palatine hill, the future site of Rome (Book VIII). 'reposcit', 'demands back': the road home lies straight through the enemy. Elision 'patri(a) alta'.

sentences.t:
Numina nulla premunt, mortali urgemur ab hoste
mortales, totidem nobis animaeque manusque.
sentences.l:
No divine powers press us; by a mortal we are pressed, by an enemy,
mortals; as many to us are both lives and hands.
sentences.i: No gods bear down on us; we are mortals hard pressed by a mortal enemy, and we have as many lives and as many hands as they have.
sentences.n: 'Numina', 'divine powers', gods. 'mortali… hoste mortales', one word set against itself across the line in two forms (polyptoton): mortals pressed by mortals. 'urgemur' picks up 'urget' two lines before (373). 'totidem nobis', 'we have as many', a dative of possession with 'sunt' understood; 'totidem', 'as many' as the enemy. '-que… -que', 'both… and'. In the Iliad Agenor steadies himself to face Achilles with the same thought: his flesh too can be pierced, he has one life, and men call him mortal (Iliad 21.568–570). Elision 'mortal(i) urgemur'.

sentences.t:
Ecce, maris magna claudit nos obice pontus,
deest iam terra fugae: pelagus Troiamne petemus?”
sentences.l:
Look, with a great barrier of sea the deep shuts us in;
there fails now land for flight: the open sea, or Troy, shall we make for?”
sentences.i: Look, the deep has shut us in behind with a great barrier of sea, and there is no more land to run across: are we to head for the open sea, or for Troy?”
sentences.n: 'maris magna… obice', 'with a great bar of sea'; 'obex' is a bolt or barrier. The Arcadians have the coast behind them. 'deest', 'is lacking', its 'de-' and 'est' run together as one syllable (synizesis). 'fugae', dative, 'for flight'. 'pelagus Troiamne', a double question with '-ne' on the second word: 'the sea, or Troy?'. 'Troy' is probably the Trojans' camp, the new Troy which the enemy is blockading, though the old city across the sea fits the irony too: either way there is nowhere to run. The Latin Library has 'petamus', a deliberative subjunctive, 'are we to make for'; Greenough's future, 'shall we make for', is plainer. The speech ends. No elisions.

sentences.t: Haec ait et medius densos prorumpit in hostis.
sentences.l: This he says, and in their midst into the packed enemy bursts.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and burst into the thick of the enemy.
sentences.n: 'Haec ait', 'this he says', the regular formula that closes a speech. 'medius', an adjective where English uses a phrase: 'in the middle', 'into their midst'. 'densos… in hostis', 'into the packed enemy', 'hostis' accusative plural in '-is'. 'prorumpit', 'bursts forward'. He does at once what he urged, cutting his way where the enemy is thickest (373). No elisions.

sentences.t:
Obvius huic primum, fatis adductus iniquis,
fit Lagus.
sentences.l:
In his way first, by the fates drawn on unjust,
is Lagus.
sentences.i: The first to cross his path, drawn on by cruel fate, was Lagus.
sentences.n: 'Obvius… fit', 'becomes in the way', meets him; 'huic', dative with 'obvius', is one syllable. 'fatis… iniquis', 'by unkind fates', ablative of means with 'adductus'. The name is held over to the next line and closes the sentence. Lagus, like most of the men killed in these battle-lists, is known only from this line: Virgil, like Homer, gives each victim a name. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Hunc, magno vellit dum pondere saxum,
intorto figit telo, discrimina costis
per medium qua spina dabat, hastamque receptat
ossibus haerentem.
sentences.l:
Him, while a rock of great weight he tears up,
with a whirled spear he pierces, where divisions to the ribs
through the middle the spine was giving, and the spear he tugs back
sticking in the bones.
sentences.i: As Lagus was wrenching up a heavy rock, Pallas hurled his spear and pierced him where the spine runs down the middle and parts the ribs, and dragged the spear back out from where it clung in the bones.
sentences.n: 'Hunc', object of 'figit'. 'dum… vellit', 'while he is tearing up'; 'magno… pondere', ablative of quality, 'of great weight': Homer's heroes, too, often snatch up a stone to throw. 'intorto… telo', 'with a whirled spear', thrown with a twist. 'discrimina costis… dabat', 'gave divisions to the ribs', 'costis' dative: the spine runs between the ribs of either side, so Lagus, stooping, is struck in the back. 'receptat', a frequentative form of 'recipio', 'tugs back' with effort, since the point sticks 'ossibus haerentem', 'clinging in the bones'. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Quem non super occupat Hisbo,
ille quidem hoc sperans:
sentences.l:
Him not standing over does Hisbo catch first,
though he indeed this was hoping:
sentences.i: Hisbo did not take Pallas by surprise as he stood over the body, though that was what he hoped:
sentences.n: 'Quem', the connecting relative, Pallas (= 'et eum'). 'super', 'above', an adverb: Pallas standing over Lagus while he frees his spear. 'occupat', 'catches first', strikes before the other can act. 'ille quidem hoc sperans', 'he indeed hoping this': Hisbo meant to catch Pallas while his weapon was stuck. The colon introduces why he failed. Elision 'quid(em) hoc'.

sentences.t:
nam Pallas ante ruentem,
dum furit, incautum crudeli morte sodalis
excipit atque ensem tumido in pulmone recondit.
sentences.i: for Pallas was ready first: as Hisbo charged, raging and careless at his comrade's cruel death, Pallas met him and buried his sword in his swelling lung.
sentences.n: 'ante', 'first', before Hisbo could strike. 'ruentem… incautum', 'rushing, off his guard', both describing Hisbo. 'dum furit', 'while he rages'. 'crudeli morte sodalis', 'at the cruel death of his comrade', ablative of cause: Hisbo was Lagus's friend. 'excipit', 'catches, meets', the word for a hunter taking a charging beast on his weapon. 'tumido… pulmone', 'the swelling lung', swollen with his fury and his panting. 'recondit', 'buries', 'hides away'. Elisions 'atqu(e) ensem', 'tumid(o) in'.

sentences.t:
Hinc Sthenium petit et Rhoeti de gente vetusta
Anchemolum, thalamos ausum incestare novercae.
sentences.l:
Next Sthenius he attacks, and of Rhoetus from the race ancient
Anchemolus, who dared the chamber to defile of his stepmother.
sentences.i: Next he went for Sthenius, and for Anchemolus, of the ancient line of Rhoetus, who had dared to defile his stepmother's bed.
sentences.n: 'Hinc', 'next'. 'Rhoeti de gente vetusta', 'of the ancient race of Rhoetus'. The old commentators tell the story: Rhoetus, a king of the Marsi, took a second wife, his son Anchemolus seduced her, and he fled his father's anger to Daunus, Turnus's father, which is why he fights here for Turnus. 'thalamos', 'the bedchamber', the plural standing for the marriage bed. 'ausum', perfect participle of 'audeo', 'having dared'. 'incestare', 'to pollute, defile'. 'novercae', 'stepmother'. Elision 'aus(um) incestare'.

sentences.i: You too fell on Rutulian fields, twin sons of Daucus, Larides and Thymber, so alike that your own family could not tell you apart, a confusion that delighted your parents;
sentences.n: The poet turns to address the twins (apostrophe), as he does with victims he pities. 'gemini', 'twins'. 'Daucia… proles', 'Daucian offspring', the sons of Daucus, an adjective from the father's name doing the work of a genitive. 'Laride', vocative of 'Larides', all three syllables long here and at 395; 'Thymber', nominative standing for the vocative, as poets allow. 'simillima', 'most alike'. 'indiscreta suis', 'indistinguishable to their own people', 'suis' dative. 'gratus… parentibus error', 'a mistake pleasing to the parents', in apposition to the whole: the mix-ups were a family joke. Greenough's 'agris' is 'arvis' in the Latin Library, to the same sense. No elisions.

sentences.t: at nunc dura dedit vobis discrimina Pallas:
sentences.l: but now harsh gave to you distinctions Pallas:
sentences.i: but now Pallas gave you a cruel way to be told apart:
sentences.n: 'dura… discrimina', 'harsh distinctions', enclosing 'dedit vobis': a grim play on the twins' likeness, since Pallas makes them different by the way he maims each of them. 'discrimina' was used at 382 of the parting of the ribs by the spine. 'dedit', perfect, 'gave'; 'vobis', dative. No elisions.

sentences.t: nam tibi, Thymbre, caput Evandrius abstulit ensis;
sentences.l: for from you, Thymber, your head Evander's took off sword;
sentences.i: for Evander's sword struck off your head, Thymber;
sentences.n: 'tibi', a dative of separation with 'abstulit', 'took away from you'. 'Thymbre', vocative. 'Evandrius… ensis', 'the Evandrian sword', the sword of Evander's house in his son's hand; the adjective from the name is used as with 'Daucia proles' just before. 'caput', 'head'. No elisions.

sentences.t:
te decisa suum, Laride, dextera quaerit
semianimesque micant digiti ferrumque retractant.
sentences.l:
you, cut off, as its own, Larides, your right hand seeks,
and half-alive twitch the fingers and the steel grasp again.
sentences.i: your severed right hand, Larides, seeks you as its master, and the half-alive fingers twitch and clutch again at the sword.
sentences.n: 'te… suum', 'you, its own': the hand looks for its owner. 'decisa', 'cut off'. 'dextera', the fuller form of 'dextra'. 'semianimes', 'half-alive', four syllables, the 'i' of 'semi-' sounded as a consonant (y). 'micant', 'flicker, twitch'. 'retractant', 'handle again', the fingers still trying to grip the sword. Ennius had already written 'semianimesque micant oculi', 'and the half-alive eyes twitch', of a severed head (Annals, quoted by the ancient commentators); Virgil reuses his line-opening. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Arcadas accensos monitu et praeclara tuentis
facta viri mixtus dolor et pudor armat in hostis.
sentences.l:
The Arcadians, fired by the warning and watching the glorious
deeds of the man, mingled grief and shame arm against the enemy.
sentences.i: The Arcadians were fired by his rebuke and by the sight of his glorious deeds, and grief and shame together armed them against the enemy.
sentences.n: 'Arcadas', Greek accusative plural, object of 'armat'. 'accensos monitu', 'kindled by his warning', the speech at 369–378. 'tuentis', accusative plural in '-is', agreeing with 'Arcadas': 'as they watch'. 'praeclara… facta viri', 'the man's glorious deeds', split across the line. 'mixtus dolor et pudor', 'grief and shame mixed', two subjects felt as one, with a singular adjective and verb. 'in hostis', 'against the enemy'. Elision 'monit(u) et'.

sentences.t:
Tum Pallas biiugis fugientem Rhoetea praeter
traicit.
sentences.l:
Then Pallas, as on his two-horse car fleeing Rhoeteus went past,
pierces him through.
sentences.i: Then, as Rhoeteus fled past in his two-horse chariot, Pallas ran him through.
sentences.n: 'biiugis', ablative of 'biiugi', 'a pair-horse chariot' (from 'bis' and 'iugum'), three syllables, the second 'i' a consonant and 'bi-' short. 'fugientem Rhoetea', 'Rhoeteus as he flees', 'Rhoetea' a Greek accusative. 'praeter', an adverb, 'past', ending the line. 'traicit' (from 'trans' and 'iacio'), three syllables, tra-i-cit, 'pierces through', held to the next line and stopped short. No elisions.

sentences.t: Hoc spatium tantumque morae fuit Ilo;
sentences.l: This space and so much of delay there was to Ilus;
sentences.i: That was all the respite and delay that Ilus won;
sentences.n: 'Hoc spatium tantumque morae', 'this interval and so much of delay', 'morae' a partitive genitive with 'tantum'. 'Ilo', dative of possession: Ilus had only this much respite. The next lines explain: the spear that killed Rhoeteus had been meant for Ilus, who lived only because Rhoeteus got in its way, and only for a moment. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Ilo namque procul validam direxerat hastam,
quam medius Rhoeteus intercipit, optime Teuthra,
te fugiens fratremque Tyren, curruque volutus
caedit semianimis Rutulorum calcibus arva.
sentences.l:
For at Ilus from afar his strong he had aimed spear,
which, coming between, Rhoeteus intercepts, noblest Teuthras,
you fleeing and your brother Tyres, and from the chariot rolled
beats, half-alive, with his heels the Rutulians' fields.
sentences.i: For Pallas had aimed his strong spear at Ilus from a distance, and Rhoeteus, coming between, caught it as he fled from you, noble Teuthras, and from your brother Tyres; rolled from his chariot, he drummed his heels, half-dead, on the Rutulians' fields.
sentences.n: 'Ilo', dative of direction, 'at Ilus'. 'direxerat', pluperfect: the spear was already in the air (the Latin Library spells it 'derexerat'). 'medius… intercipit', 'in between, he intercepts'. 'optime Teuthra', vocative: the poet turns to address an Arcadian, from whom, with his brother 'Tyren' (Greek accusative of 'Tyres'), Rhoeteus was fleeing. 'Rhoeteus' has 'eu' as one syllable. 'curru volutus', 'rolled from the chariot', 'curru' ablative of separation. 'caedit… calcibus arva', 'strikes the ground with his heels', his death-throes; 'semianimis' as at 396. 'Rutulorum… arva', the Rutulians' own soil. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Ac velut optato ventis aestate coortis
dispersa immittit silvis incendia pastor,
correptis subito mediis extenditur una
horrida per latos acies Volcania campos;
ille sedens victor flammas despectat ovantis:
sentences.l:
And as, at his wish, the winds in summer having risen,
scattered fires into the woods sends a shepherd,
the parts between suddenly seized, there spreads out, one,
bristling over the broad plains, the battle-line of Vulcan;
he, sitting as victor, looks down on the flames exulting:
sentences.i: And as in summer, once the winds he has waited for spring up, a shepherd sets fire to the woods at scattered points; all at once the spaces between are caught, and Vulcan's battle-line spreads out in one bristling front across the broad plains, while he sits, a victor, gazing down on the flames as they exult:
sentences.n: The simile. 'optato', ablative used as an adverb, 'as he wished'; 'ventis… coortis', ablative absolute, 'the winds having risen'. 'dispersa… incendia', 'scattered fires', set at several points; 'immittit silvis', 'sends into the woods', dative with a compound verb. Shepherds burned off scrub to bring up fresh pasture. 'correptis… mediis', ablative absolute, 'the spaces between being caught'. 'acies Volcania', 'Vulcan's battle-line', the fire-front pictured as an army, the god's name standing for fire. 'ovantis', accusative plural in '-is', 'exulting', as soldiers cheer at a triumph. The scattered fires that join in one line are Pallas's men, rallied. Homer likens a hero's onslaught to fire racing through a wood (Iliad 11.155–157; 20.490–492). Elision 'dispers(a) immittit'.

sentences.t:
non aliter socium virtus coit omnis in unum
teque iuvat, Palla.
sentences.l:
not otherwise of your comrades the valour comes together, all, into one
and helps you, Pallas.
sentences.i: just so the courage of all your comrades gathered into one and came to your aid, Pallas.
sentences.n: 'non aliter', 'not otherwise', closes the simile. 'socium' = 'sociorum', the old genitive plural. 'coit… in unum', 'comes together into one', as the scattered fires merged into a single front. 'omnis', nominative singular with 'virtus', 'all the valour'. 'Palla', Greek vocative of 'Pallas': the poet turns to address him, as he addresses those he pities, a quiet hint of what is coming. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Sed bellis acer Halaesus
tendit in adversos seque in sua conligit arma.
sentences.l:
But in wars keen Halaesus
heads against those facing him, and himself into his own gathers armour.
sentences.i: But Halaesus, fierce in war, pressed forward against them, gathering himself behind his shield.
sentences.n: Halaesus was introduced at 352 in the last part; in the catalogue of Book VII he is 'Agamemnonius', of Agamemnon's house or following, an enemy of the Trojan name (VII.723). 'bellis acer', 'keen in wars', ablative of respect. 'tendit in adversos', 'makes for those facing him'. 'se… in sua conligit arma', 'gathers himself into his arms', crouches behind his shield ready to strike; 'conligit' is Greenough's spelling of 'colligit', which the Latin Library prints. Elision 'sequ(e) in'.

sentences.t:
Hic mactat Ladona Pheretaque Demodocumque,
Strymonio dextram fulgenti deripit ense
elatam in iugulum, saxo ferit ora Thoantis
ossaque dispersit cerebro permixta cruento.
sentences.i: He slew Ladon, Pheres and Demodocus; with his flashing sword he lopped off the right hand of Strymonius as it was raised against his throat; he struck Thoas in the face with a stone and scattered his bones, mixed with blood and brains.
sentences.n: 'Hic', 'he', Halaesus. 'mactat', 'slaughters', properly a word of sacrifice. 'Ladona', 'Phereta', Greek accusatives (La-do-na with its first two syllables long, Phe-re-ta with its first short); '-que… -que' joins the three names. 'Strymonio', dative of separation, 'from Strymonius'. 'deripit', 'tears away'. 'elatam in iugulum', 'raised against the throat', Halaesus's throat: Strymonius was about to strike. 'ora', 'face', plural for singular. 'dispersit', a perfect among presents, the instant result. 'cerebro… cruento', 'with bloody brain', ablative with 'permixta'. Several names are Homeric: Thoas, and Demodocus, the Phaeacian bard of the Odyssey. Elision 'elat(am) in'.

sentences.t: Fata canens silvis genitor celarat Halaesum:
sentences.l: Singing the fates, in the woods his father had hidden Halaesus:
sentences.i: His father, who could foretell the fates, had hidden Halaesus away in the woods;
sentences.n: 'Fata canens', 'singing the fates', prophesying: his father was a seer who foresaw that the boy would die in war. 'silvis', ablative of place, 'in the woods'. 'celarat' = 'celaverat', the shortened pluperfect. Homer's seer Merops of Percote likewise tried to keep his two sons from the war, and they went and died (Iliad 2.831–834; 11.329–332). No elisions.

sentences.t:
ut senior leto canentia lumina solvit,
iniecere manum Parcae telisque sacrarunt
Evandri.
sentences.l:
when the old man in death his whitening eyes released,
laid hand on him the Fates, and to the weapons devoted him
of Evander.
sentences.i: but when the old man's eyes, grown white with age, were closed in death, the Fates laid their hand on Halaesus and devoted him to the weapons of Evander.
sentences.n: 'ut', 'when', with the perfect. 'senior', 'the old man'. 'leto', ablative, 'in death'. 'canentia lumina', 'whitening eyes', from 'caneo' (long 'a', as in 'canus'), 'to be grey or white': dim with age, a play on 'canens', 'singing' (short 'a', from 'cano'), in the line before. 'solvit', 'released'. 'iniecere' = 'iniecerunt', with consonantal 'i' after the prefix. 'manum inicere', 'to lay a hand on', a Roman legal phrase for seizing what one claims as one's own. 'Parcae', the Fates. 'sacrarunt' = 'sacraverunt', 'consecrated', marked him as a victim. 'Evandri' is held to the next line: the weapons are those of Evander's son. No elisions.

sentences.t: Quem sic Pallas petit ante precatus:
sentences.l: Him thus Pallas attacks, having first prayed:
sentences.i: Before he attacked him, Pallas prayed in these words:
sentences.n: 'Quem', connecting relative, 'and him' (= 'et eum'), Halaesus. 'petit', 'attacks', 'aims at'. 'ante precatus', 'having first prayed', the perfect participle of the deponent 'precor' with 'ante' as an adverb. 'sic', 'thus', points to the prayer that follows. No elisions.

sentences.t:
“Da nunc, Thybri pater, ferro, quod missile libro,
fortunam atque viam duri per pectus Halaesi.
sentences.l:
“Grant now, father Tiber, to the steel which, to throw, I poise,
fortune and a way through the breast of hard Halaesus.
sentences.i: “Grant now, Father Tiber, to the steel I balance for the throw, good fortune and a path through the breast of hard Halaesus.
sentences.n: Pallas prays to the river Tiber, god of the land, on whose bank Evander's town stands; Tiberinus appeared to Aeneas in Book VIII. 'Thybri', vocative of 'Thybris', the Greek-style form of the river's name. 'ferro', dative, 'to the steel', the spear's point. 'quod missile libro', 'which I poise as a missile', 'libro' to balance a weapon before throwing it, 'missile' predicative. 'fortunam atque viam', 'success and a passage'. 'duri', 'hard', unyielding. Elision 'fortun(am) atque'.

sentences.t: Haec arma exuviasque viri tua quercus habebit.”
sentences.l: These arms and spoils of the man your oak will have.”
sentences.i: Your oak shall have these arms and this man's spoils.”
sentences.n: The vow: if the god grants success, Pallas will hang Halaesus's armour on an oak by the river, sacred to the god, as victors dedicated spoils on a tree as a trophy. 'exuviae', 'spoils', what is stripped from the body. 'tua quercus', 'your oak', the tree on the Tiber's bank. The thought of spoils is ironic: later in this book Turnus will strip the sword-belt from Pallas's own body. Elision 'arm(a) exuviasque'. The speech ends.

sentences.t: Audiit illa deus:
sentences.l: Heard those words the god:
sentences.i: The god heard his prayer:
sentences.n: 'Audiit' = 'audivit', the perfect with its 'v' dropped. 'illa', 'those things', the words of the prayer, neuter plural. 'deus', the Tiber. The answer comes at once, in the half-line before the colon; not every prayer in the poem is granted, and Pallas's next one, to Hercules, will not be. No elisions.

sentences.t:
dum texit Imaona Halaesus,
Arcadio infelix telo dat pectus inermum.
sentences.l:
while he shielded Imaon, Halaesus
to the Arcadian, ill-starred, spear gives his breast unprotected.
sentences.i: for while Halaesus was covering Imaon, the luckless man laid his unguarded breast open to the Arcadian spear.
sentences.n: 'dum texit', 'while he shielded', perfect of 'tego' (the present is 'tegit'): 'dum' normally takes the present, and the perfect here is unusual. 'Imaona', Greek accusative of 'Imaon', one of his comrades. 'Arcadio… telo', 'to the Arcadian spear', Pallas's, dative. 'infelix', 'ill-starred'. 'inermum', 'unarmed, unprotected', a by-form of 'inermis'. In shielding a friend Halaesus exposes himself, and the fate laid on him at 419 is fulfilled. Elisions 'Imaon(a) Halaesus', 'Arcadi(o) infelix'.

sentences.t:
At non caede viri tanta perterrita Lausus,
pars ingens belli, sinit agmina:
sentences.l:
But not, by the slaughter of so great a man, terrified does Lausus,
a huge part of the war, suffer the columns to be:
sentences.i: But Lausus, a mighty part of the war himself, would not let the ranks lose heart at the death of so great a man:
sentences.n: Lausus is the son of the Etruscan exile Mezentius, Turnus's ally; in the catalogue of Book VII he is second in beauty only to Turnus. 'perterrita… sinit agmina', 'does not let the columns (be) terrified', the participle predicative with 'sinit'; 'non' goes with 'sinit'. 'caede viri tanta', 'by the slaughter of so great a man', ablative of cause, Halaesus's death. 'pars ingens belli', 'a huge part of the war', in apposition: a mainstay of his side. No elisions.

sentences.t:
primus Abantem
oppositum interimit, pugnae nodumque moramque.
sentences.l:
first Abas,
set against him, he kills, of the fight both the knot and the stay.
sentences.i: First he killed Abas, who stood in his way, the knot on which the fighting had snagged and stood still.
sentences.n: 'primus', 'first', an adjective where English uses an adverb. 'Abantem', accusative of 'Abas', an Etruscan captain from the catalogue of Aeneas's allies earlier in this book. 'oppositum', 'set against him'. 'interimit', 'kills'. 'pugnae nodumque moramque', 'both knot and delay of the fight', in apposition: Abas was the point where the battle was tied up and held back, the man the enemy could not get past. '-que… -que'. Elision 'opposit(um) interimit'.

sentences.t:
Sternitur Arcadiae proles, sternuntur Etrusci
et vos, O Grais imperdita corpora, Teucri.
sentences.l:
Laid low is Arcadia's offspring, laid low the Etruscans,
and you, O by the Greeks undestroyed bodies, Teucrians.
sentences.i: Down go the sons of Arcadia, down go the Etruscans, and you too, Trojans, whose bodies the Greeks could not destroy.
sentences.n: 'Sternitur… sternuntur', the same verb opening each clause (anaphora), singular with 'proles', plural with 'Etrusci'. 'Arcadiae proles', 'the offspring of Arcadia', Pallas's men. 'Etrusci', Tarchon's Etruscans, Aeneas's allies. Then the poet addresses the Trojans themselves. 'Grais imperdita corpora', 'bodies not destroyed by the Greeks', 'Grais' (two long syllables, Gra-is) a dative of agent with the participle; 'imperdita' appears to be Virgil's own coinage. They survived the sack of Troy only to die here. 'Teucri', 'Teucrians', with 'eu' one syllable. No elisions.

sentences.t: Agmina concurrunt ducibusque et viribus aequis.
sentences.l: The columns clash, with leaders and strength equal.
sentences.i: The armies came together, matched in their leaders and in their strength.
sentences.n: 'concurrunt', 'run together', the word for armies meeting. 'ducibus… et viribus aequis', ablative of manner, 'with leaders and strength equal', 'aequis' going with both nouns. The leaders who balance each other are Pallas and Lausus, as the next lines show. Elision 'ducibusqu(e) et'.

sentences.t:
Extremi addensent acies nec turba moveri
tela manusque sinit.
sentences.l:
The rearmost pack the lines tight, nor does the crowd to be moved
weapons and hands allow.
sentences.i: The rear ranks press the lines together, and the crush is too thick for anyone to move a weapon or a hand.
sentences.n: 'Extremi', 'the hindmost', the rear ranks pushing forward. 'addensent', 'make thick', a rare verb, from 'addenseo'. 'acies', accusative plural, 'the lines'. 'turba', 'the crush', subject of 'sinit'. 'tela manusque moveri', 'weapons and hands to be moved', accusative and infinitive after 'sinit', with 'nec' going with the verb. Compare the press at the close of the last part, foot against foot (361). Elision 'Extrem(i) addensent'.

sentences.t:
Hinc Pallas instat et urget,
hinc contra Lausus, nec multum discrepat aetas:
sentences.l:
On this side Pallas presses and drives on,
on that side, facing him, Lausus, nor much differs their age:
sentences.i: On one side Pallas pushes forward and drives on, on the other Lausus stands against him, and there is little difference in their years:
sentences.n: 'Hinc… hinc', 'on this side… on that side'. 'instat et urget', two nearly synonymous verbs for steady pressure, understood again with 'Lausus'. 'contra', 'facing', 'opposite'. 'nec multum discrepat aetas', 'nor does their age differ much': both are young men, and both are sons fighting in the sight of armies led by or allied with their fathers. No elisions.

sentences.t:
egregii forma, sed quis Fortuna negarat
in patriam reditus.
sentences.l:
outstanding in beauty, but to whom Fortune had denied
into their homeland returns.
sentences.i: both of them strikingly fair, but Fortune had refused them any homecoming.
sentences.n: 'egregii forma', 'outstanding in form', ablative of respect, 'egregii' nominative plural. 'quis' = 'quibus', the old dative plural of the relative, as at 366: 'to whom'. 'Fortuna', capitalised as the goddess. 'negarat' = 'negaverat', the shortened pluperfect. 'reditus', accusative plural, 'returns', one for each. The poet tells us their deaths before they happen: both will fall in this book. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Ipsos concurrere passus
haud tamen inter se magni regnator Olympi:
sentences.l:
Them to clash, however, did not allow
with each other the ruler of great Olympus:
sentences.i: Yet the ruler of great Olympus would not allow the two to clash with one another:
sentences.n: 'Ipsos', 'the two themselves', set first for emphasis. 'concurrere passus haud', 'did not allow to clash', 'passus' (est) from the deponent 'patior', with the accusative and infinitive. 'tamen', 'however'. 'inter se', 'with each other'. 'magni regnator Olympi', 'the ruler of great Olympus', Jupiter, held back to the end of the line. No elisions.

sentences.t: mox illos sua fata manent maiore sub hoste.
sentences.l: soon them their own fates await under a greater enemy.
sentences.i: soon each of them was to meet his own death at the hands of a greater enemy.
sentences.n: 'mox', 'soon'. 'sua fata', 'their own fates', each his own. 'manent', 'await'. 'maiore sub hoste', 'under a greater foe', 'sub' with the ablative, at his hands: Pallas will die by Turnus, and Lausus by Aeneas, later in this book. The part ends on that forecast. No elisions.
